analysis.one_liner: Makes executives and large shareholders of failed big banks repay up to three years of compensation.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan backing from 13 senators, the bill never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDIC, when a large bank (over $10 billion in assets) fails, to take back up to three years of compensation from executives, directors, and large shareholders who caused the failure — including salary, bonuses, stock awards, and profits from buying or selling the bank's securities. The recovered money would go into the federal Deposit Insurance Fund, which backs ordinary people's bank accounts. It would also broaden the FDIC's existing power to claw back pay when it takes over a failing financial company.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, whose federally backed Deposit Insurance Fund absorbs losses when big banks fail and would be repaid first from executives' clawed-back pay. The FDIC gains a clear, mandatory tool to recover money from the people responsible for a failure instead of leaving those losses with the insurance fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors, taxpayers, and the FDIC insurance fund

how_it_helps.text: When a bank with more than $10 billion in assets fails, the FDIC would be required to claw back covered compensation — salary, bonuses, performance and equity awards, and profits from buying or selling securities — from executives, directors, and other parties who caused more than a minimal financial loss to the bank.

All clawed-back money would be deposited into the Deposit Insurance Fund, the fund that protects ordinary Americans' bank deposits, so the people who caused the failure — not the insurance fund backed by the banking system — would absorb the loss.

The bill would also expand the FDIC's authority under Dodd-Frank to claw back compensation from parties responsible for losses at a failed financial company, no matter which legal process put the FDIC in charge.

analysis.who_pays: Executives, directors, controlling stockholders, and other participants in the affairs of failed banks with over $10 billion in assets, who would surrender up to three years of compensation — including stock gains — after a failure they helped cause.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and big shareholders of failed banks

drawbacks.text: The definition of who can be forced to repay is broad: it reaches not just officers and directors but any shareholder, joint venture partner, or other person the regulators decide 'participates in the conduct of the affairs' of the bank, so people with limited day-to-day control could still be on the hook if they contributed to a significant loss.

Clawing back three years of salary, equity awards, and securities-trading profits after any failure could make it harder for large banks to recruit and retain directors and executives willing to accept that personal financial exposure — a cost honest supporters of accountability would acknowledge.

The trigger is 'more than a minimal financial loss' or a 'significant adverse effect,' which leaves regulators substantial discretion over who pays and how much, creating uncertainty about how the law would be applied in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is straightforward and aimed at a real problem: after high-profile bank failures, executives kept pay earned while their banks collapsed and the government-insured fund covered the losses. Making the people responsible repay up to three years of compensation shifts those losses back to them. The main cost is breadth and uncertainty — the liability net extends beyond top executives to shareholders and other participants, and the vague loss threshold gives regulators wide discretion — but for ordinary depositors and the insurance fund the trade-off is favorable.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Failed Bank Executives Clawback Act on June 1, 2023, with 12 cosponsors — 7 Democrats and 5 Republicans — including Senators Hawley, Vance, Braun, Britt, and Cramer.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs that same day.
The referral was the bill's last action; the Banking Committee never took it up, and it never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives, directors, and large shareholders of failed large banks are better off: no law requires them to repay compensation after a failure. The Deposit Insurance Fund and the depositors it protects gain nothing that the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank executives and large shareholders of failed banks

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 12 cosponsors split 7 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but the bill never got any roll-call vote, so there is no recorded vote split.

industries.industry: Executives, directors, and controlling shareholders of large banks (over $10B in assets)
industries.note: The bill targets this group directly: after a bank failure they caused, they would surrender up to three years of compensation, including stock-sale profits, to the Deposit Insurance Fund. Their interest in keeping that compensation runs directly against depositors and the insurance fund that would otherwise absorb the losses.

The rules only bite after a failure, so healthy banks would see no day-to-day change, but the prospect of mandatory clawbacks raises the personal financial risk of running a big bank and could push up the compensation needed to attract bank leadership. Ordinary depositors are protected either way; the industry's incentive to avoid failure-causing risk-taking aligns with the public's.

The fund that guarantees ordinary Americans' deposits would receive all clawed-back compensation, recovering money after failures that it currently absorbs. Because the bill died, the fund gains nothing.
